title: Data: Revenue Isn't Cash, and Neither Is Paper Profit
summary: Notes on the Cash chapter of Data: why a company that sells well and shows a profit can still run short, how growth eats cash, and how to give each cash driver one owner.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: Data
book.originalTitle: Data: Harness Your Numbers to Go from Uncertain to Unstoppable
book.note: This article is a practical reflection on the book within the EOS context. It is not a substitute for reading the original work.

html:
End of the month, sales has good news: three big contracts signed and revenue ahead of plan. Everyone celebrates. Two weeks later the accountant messages the CEO privately. Payroll next month will be tight, the biggest customer still hasn't paid the last invoice, and the new project has already needed extra hires. On the report everything looks great. In the bank account it doesn't.

Chapter 5 of Data, the EOS book by Mark O'Donnell, Angela Kalemis and Mark Stanley, has a one-word title: Cash (table of contents). This is the fourth post in my series on the book, after the opener, the Scorecard and Everyone Has a Number. The chapter's point sounds old: revenue isn't cash, and profit on paper isn't cash either. Plenty of teams still run as if all three were the same number.

Sales, profit and cash are three different things

  • Revenue is what customers agreed to pay you. Agreed, which isn't the same as paid.
  • Profit is what's left after expenses, the way accounting records it.
  • Cash is money actually in the account, ready to cover salaries, suppliers and loans today.

HBS Online defines cash flow as "the net balance of cash moving into and out of a business at a specific point in time," and points out that "it's possible for a company to be both profitable and have a negative cash flow" (Cash Flow vs. Profit). The gap is timing. Under the accrual method, as the US Small Business Administration explains, a sale goes on the books when it's completed, while the cash method records it only when payment arrives (Manage your finances). So a P&L can look healthy for months while the bank balance lags behind.

A simple example makes it concrete. Say you win a $100,000 project. Delivering it costs $70,000, mostly salaries and licenses, spread over the first two months. The customer pays in full in month four. On paper the project makes $30,000. Here's what the bank account sees:

MonthCash outCash inBalance vs. start
1$35,0000−$35,000
2$35,0000−$70,000
300−$70,000
40$100,000+$30,000

The project really is profitable, and the company still carries $70,000 of its own money for three months. Win two of these at once and it's $140,000. That's how a company that sells well ends up worrying about payroll.

Growth eats cash

It sounds backwards, but growing faster can drain cash faster. In a 2001 Harvard Business Review article, Neil Churchill and John Mullins warned that "a profitable company that tries to grow too fast can run out of cash" (How Fast Can Your Company Afford to Grow?). The project above shows the mechanism. You hire first, buy first, pay commission first and set up infrastructure first, and the customer's money shows up later. The more work you take on, the deeper that hole gets.

Growth is still worth chasing. Just draw the hole before you jump in: how deep it is, how long it lasts, which month cash turns positive again, and what has to be true for the plan to be more than hope. A deal that looks great on the revenue line can look a lot less great once payment terms, margin and delivery effort sit on the same page.

Everyone touches cash

Many teams treat money as finance's problem. Sales sells, operations delivers, support keeps customers happy. In practice every function leaves fingerprints on cash:

  • When sales picks customers who pay late or closes with a discount, it's deciding when money arrives and how much of it is left.
  • Delivery chips away at a project's margin every time work gets redone.
  • If contracts bill from go-live, an implementation team that gets customers live sooner also gets invoices out sooner.
  • A product team that ships fewer bugs also triggers fewer refunds and support tickets.
  • Whoever cancels the tool subscription nobody uses saves real cash next month.

Nobody outside finance needs to read statements like a CFO. Anyone running part of the business should still know how the company makes money, where cash gets stuck and how their own work connects to it. How much of the numbers you open up is each company's call. At minimum, the leadership team should trust each other enough to talk about cash honestly.

The Cash chapter's main tool for this is an exercise called Cash Flow Drivers. Ninety's write-up of the exercise (Cash Flow Doesn't Just Happen, You Drive It) lays out the steps roughly like this:

  1. The leadership team brainstorms everything that moves cash and profit, then narrows it to the 6 to 10 drivers that matter most right now. Examples include sales conversion, inventory turns, price realization, labor utilization, receivables and payables timing, and rework or returns.
  2. Each driver gets exactly one owner. In the write-up's words: "Not a department. Not a team. A single owner."
  3. Each owner sets an improvement goal. The examples given are raising gross margin from 42% to 45%, collecting 10 days faster, or keeping rework under 2% of orders.
  4. The drivers go onto the Scorecard, with quarterly Rocks and weekly to-dos to move them.
  5. The team revisits the list at least once a year.

What I like about it is that it pulls money out of the accountant's spreadsheet and onto the weekly meeting agenda, with a name, a number and a deadline. A detailed financial model helps you calculate and run scenarios. It can't tell you who's fixing what this week. If your team already runs a Scorecard, cash drivers are just a few more rows.

Small leaks add up

Cash problems don't always come from one big mistake. Often they come from small leaks that repeat: a bit of rework every week, a discount handed out "to close faster," a customer who always pays late, a manual cleanup step nobody automated, a subscription nobody uses and nobody cancels.

Discounts are worth doing the math on. Say an item sells for $100 and costs $70, so gross profit is $30. Sales offers 5% off to close the deal. Now the price is $95 and gross profit is $25. To earn the same total gross profit as before, you have to sell 20% more units. "Sure, 5% off" sounds tiny. The number behind it isn't.

Each leak looks too small to bother with, which is exactly why it survives. Tracking a few of them every week lets the team spot the pattern before it becomes normal. A cash-aware company doesn't have to turn stingy. It gets more deliberate about where to spend, where to invest and where a small process fix would pay back more than another heroic push.

Cash buys you room to choose

Cash shapes how leaders decide. A company with a buffer can turn down a bad deal, hire carefully, invest patiently and negotiate from a stronger position. A company without one tends to react. It accepts poor terms, rushes hires, cuts in the wrong places or keeps putting off decisions because every option feels dangerous.

None of this means hoarding cash out of fear. Money sitting idle with no plan is wasted, and so is money spent because it looked like there was plenty. Cash should serve the strategy, and that only works when the whole leadership team can see it clearly.

What I want to keep

Cash flow is the sum of hundreds of small decisions in sales, operations, service, hiring, pricing and collections. Finance just gets to see it first.

Try this week

  • Ask your accountant one question: if no new money came in from today, how many months of payroll and fixed costs could we cover?
  • Take your biggest active contract and map its cash month by month, like the table above.
  • Before the next discount, work out how many more units you'd need to sell to keep total gross profit flat.
  • List three things your team does that affect cash: collections, rework, expenses, pricing or payment terms.
  • If your team runs a Scorecard, add one cash driver and give it to exactly one person.

faqs.q: What's the difference between revenue, profit and cash?
faqs.a: Revenue is what customers agreed to pay. Profit is what's left after expenses, the way accounting records it. Cash is the money actually in the account to pay salaries and suppliers today. The three are related, but they often disagree on timing.

faqs.q: How can a profitable company run out of cash?
faqs.a: Money usually goes out before it comes in. A $100,000 project that costs $70,000 over its first two months and gets paid in month four still makes $30,000, but the company carries $70,000 for three months. Neil Churchill and John Mullins made the same point in Harvard Business Review in 2001: a profitable company that grows too fast can run out of cash.

faqs.q: What are Cash Flow Drivers in the Data book?
faqs.a: It's an exercise from Chapter 5 (Cash) of Data. The leadership team lists what moves cash and profit, narrows it to the 6 to 10 drivers that matter most, gives each driver a single owner and an improvement goal, and tracks them on the weekly Scorecard.

faqs.q: Do people outside finance need to understand cash flow?
faqs.a: Yes, at a basic level. Nobody needs to read statements like a CFO, but anyone running part of the business should know how the company makes money, where cash gets stuck and how their work affects it. Picking late-paying customers, discounting, rework and go-live dates all touch cash.

faqs.q: How much does a 5% discount really cost?
faqs.a: More than it looks. An item that sells for $100 and costs $70 earns $30 of gross profit. At 5% off it earns $25, so you need to sell 20% more units just to keep total gross profit where it was.
